title: When the Chameleon Carried the Word
summary: uNkulunkulu sends the slow chameleon with a word of life, but a hurried lizard runs ahead with another word that changes everything.
moral: A word carried in haste cannot be called back; a gentle word outlives it.
attribution: A traditional Zulu tale, retold for Ubuntu Tales.

cover.alt: A slow chameleon on a branch before a wide saffron sun, with hills layered in terracotta

sentences.text: In the beginning, before the rivers had learned their courses and before the hills had been given their names, uNkulunkulu looked down from above the sky.
He saw a wide world, and on it were people, and they were quiet.
Their tongues had no stories in them yet, and they did not know why they had been made.
uNkulunkulu called the chameleon to his side.
The chameleon was slow-footed and patient, and it wore the colours of leaves and stone so well that the wind could pass by without noticing it.
“Carry a word to the people,” uNkulunkulu said.
“Tell them that they will live, and that the grave will not keep them.”
The chameleon nodded and set off down the long road, one careful foot after another.
It did not run.
It stopped to look at the sky.
It greeted an old tortoise and listened to the water in the valley.
The world was new, and the chameleon saw no reason to hurry past it.
Now the lizard had been watching from the shade of a flat rock, and it was not pleased.
“The chameleon will take a whole season to arrive,” the lizard said to itself.
“The people will still be waiting when the mountains grow old.
I will run ahead and make myself useful.”
So the lizard ran, quick as a thrown stone, down the hills and through the valleys.
It reached the people before the chameleon had even crossed the first river.
“Listen!”
the lizard cried.
“The word has been given to me.
You will live for a while, and then you will die, and the earth will take you back.”
The people wept.
They had never heard of death before, and the idea of it moved through them like a cold wind.
That night they built their first fires to keep the darkness from coming too close, and the old ones began to count the days.
The chameleon was late because it had stopped to eat a fruit that hung low over the path.
It was still chewing when it heard the people wailing.
“What has happened here?”
it asked, and the lizard flicked its tail and looked away.
When the chameleon finally stood before the people, it told them the word it had been given: that they would live, and that the grave would not keep them.
But the people had already taken the other word into their mouths, and a word spoken over a whole people is not easily called back.
uNkulunkulu heard the weeping and understood what had been done.
He did not strike the lizard down, and he did not make the chameleon run faster.
He looked at the people for a long time, and then he said, “If death will walk with them, then let life walk closer.”
So the people learned to hold two things at once.
They learned that they would die, and they learned that this was exactly why a bowl of food shared at dusk, a child’s first laugh and a story told beside the fire were precious.
They began to give each other what they had, and to say the names of those who had gone.
When an old person died, the people did not only weep.
They sat together and told the story of the word that had been carried badly, and then they told the story of the person’s life, with all its small kindnesses set out in order.
In this way death taught them to remember, and remembering taught them to be gentle with one another.
The chameleon still walks slowly, changing colour as it goes.
Some say it is still carrying the first word, looking for a time and a people patient enough to hear it.
Others say it is only looking for the fruit it never finished.
Either way, it is in no hurry, and the world has not yet run out of people who need the message.
That is why the old people say: do not hurry a gentle thing.
A word carried in peace can outlive a word carried in haste, and a people who remember death will make room for life.
